17214.content:
The book starts with Johnnie being brainwashed into being a career soldier even though he doesn't want to.

Throughout his training he reflects upon radical ideas of militarism as if he doesn't belong in such a word. The text gives you subtle hints (nothing more) of how different this world is from the time the book was written. You even see predictions of things wrong with today's society. What I expected was for the protagonist (or any other character) to understand gradually that this isn't how things should be;or that there might be a better way. But, no.

The military works, the beatings are successfull without reoffence, Rico's thoughts and objections are silenced and he becomes a proper bootlicker for the army even before he learns about the eventual conscription of his father. 

Their enemy is brutal and unforgiving, as far away as a thing can be from a human physically and culturally. The arachnids/bugs are ruthless creatures without individuality, willing to sacrifice themselves and their kind for the death of one human. 

Since all the adversaries of the Terran Empire (or whatever) are represented as purely evil, the reader doesn't even get a chance to process the possibility of them being redeemable.

---

50902608.content:
TLDR; While it has very interesting plot points and conflicts that can go to interesting directions, the plot progresses too slowly when its uninteresting and too fast when it feels important. The ending just happens while Robert does nothing.

I think this book displays the SF writers' obsession with the 'science' and leaving the 'fiction' part to take care of itself, somehow. 

---

The book begins with the whole world already dead and poor ol' Robert surviving alone in the aftermath. He is slowly getting accustomed to the notion of being alone, struggling with loneliness, the loss of his family and a bit of survivor's guilt on top of all. He hates every moment of it.

Every night his neighbors and his old friend/ co-worker Ben Cortman; the absolute chad that he is; pile up in front of his house, calling his name with the sole purpose of killing him / drinking his blood / maybe making him a vampire, I'm not entirely sure. Robert Neville has taken his precautions, he knows that they don't like the smell of garlic, some of them can't stand seeing a cross and most importantly, he knows how to kill them for good. He also knows that they want him desperately, patiently and eagerly waiting for his resolve to diminish so that they can get to him. 

The vampires aren't smart, but boy are they determined. Ben calls out his name repeatedly, the others constantly harass him, keep him awake and alert unless he surpresses their noise. They throw bricks at his house, the windows already replaced with wooden planks, the door fortified, houses around his own he has already burnt down. Every single precaution he can think of and act upon are already made. He has nothing left to do, nothing more to think, to listen to. This cycle repeats every night, and Robert is slowly losing ground, retreating into his shell to avoid them.

"*He could still see them out there, the white-faced men prowling around his house, looking ceaselessly for a way to get in at him. [...] eyes glittering at the house, teeth slowly grating together, back and forth, back and forth.

*And the women…

*Did he have to start thinking about them again? [...] Let the morning come. His mind spoke the words it spoke every night, Dear God, let the morning come.*"

They know who he is and what he is living through. I think, **they know** that if they keep this up for a while, they will get him. Night begins, Ben yells "Come out, Neville!" and Robert briefly defies them, overthinks, starts drinking and finally shuts down from mental exhaustion.

Then the sun dawns.

During the day Robert has to deal with whatever bullshittery has happened the night before, he nails planks to wherever they broke around the house, takes care of the garlic hothouse*, makes round trips to get the supplies needed. He hates every part of this routine, the monotonous work, the smell of garlic on his hands, his food, his drinks. Most of all he hates being alone. He grieves for his wife and daughter and sometimes he questions the point of survival in a world without them. Then he drives recklessly, kills every vampire he comes across — who regularly put themselves in a sleep-like coma during the day. At this point in the story the most probable cause of his death would come from his own two hands.

My boy is depressed, alone and hopeless. 

He mourns his wife Virginia, whom he saw die twice; once by the plague and once by his own hand. He mourns his daughter Kathy, he regrets allowing her to be burned after her untimely death.??

My boy is depressed and horny as fuck, longing for a meaningful connection while trying to keep the intrusive thoughts away. Robert Neville has been through some things. Robert Neville is thinking of ending said things. He nearly does it in Chapter Three; 

*"His throat moved and a shaking breath passed his lips. Come out. The women were out there, their dresses open or taken off, their flesh waiting for his touch, their lips waiting for-My blood, my blood!"*

So; wake up, brush your teeth, do some boring tasks, maybe drive around a bit, get home to be harassed by dead perverts, drink yourself to sleep. This routine would drive anyone crazy, and it has taken it's toll on Robert as well. 



*Garlic. Everywhere the smell of garlic. In his clothes and in the furniture and in his food and even in his drink.*

*Reading-drinking-soundproof-the-house-the women. The women, the lustful, bloodthirsty, naked women flaunting their hot bodies at him. No, not hot. 

*A shuddering whine wrenched up through his chest and throat. Goddamn them, what were they waiting for? Did they think he was going to come out and hand himself over?

*Maybe I am, maybe I am. He actually found himself jerking off the crossbar from the door. Coming, girls, I’m coming. Wet your lips, now.*
